text: INFORME SEMANAL JJ. MONTOYA. SPX: la volatilidad despierta, el VIX entra en backwardation y aumenta el riesgo de nuevas caídas. Análisis del mercado: 👉🔗📌⬇️⬇️⬇️ https://jjmontoya.substack.com/p/informe-semanal-jj-montoya-spx-la-dbb?r=3q4ztp&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&showWelcomeOnShare=true ⚡ TL;DR El S&P 500 cayó un 1% y el Nasdaq 100 retrocedió un 3% durante la jornada de OPEX, en una sesión marcada por un fuerte deterioro del sentimiento y una expansión significativa de la volatilidad. El VIX se disparó un 23%, llegando a tocar los 22 puntos intradía, su nivel más alto en más de cuatro meses. Por su parte, el VVIX repuntó un 20%, hasta 110, reflejando un importante encarecimiento de las opciones sobre el propio VIX. Las volatilidades implícitas del SPX a strikes fijos también aumentaron con fuerza, confirmando que los operadores comenzaron a pagar más por protección. Pero la señal más relevante llegó desde la estructura temporal de la volatilidad: la curva de futuros del VIX entró en backwardation, una configuración asociada a una mayor tensión y a una elevada demanda de protección inmediata. El mercado entra ahora en una ventana especialmente delicada, con el OPEX de octubre ya superado y el vencimiento del VIX la próxima semana. 👉 La principal preocupación es que una continuación de las caídas provoque una búsqueda urgente de coberturas por parte de inversores que actualmente mantienen poca protección. Esa demanda podría alimentar nuevas compras de puts, elevar la volatilidad y provocar ventas adicionales de futuros por parte de dealers cortos de gamma. Por ahora, las referencias más importantes son 7.650 como primera defensa, 7.700 como nivel a recuperar y 7.500–7.450 como siguientes zonas bajistas.

Onshore China stocks gunning for 11 weeks straight of going down. China stocks in the doghouse. My high level thoughts: - short/medium term, the China trade is a essentially a geopolitical uncertainty index trade. The more uncertain the geopolitical climate, the worse Chinese equities do (valuations be damned), and geopolitics is as uncertain as it gets right now. What's curious though is the Chinese Yuan has been on a ripper (vs. USD at least), but that's a discussion for some other time.. - the long-term bull case for China basically boils down to when do equity market returns 'catch up' to GDP growth? How does a country's economy grow so spectacularly while its equity markets perform so badly? Shouldn't they be aligned? China Real GDP CAGR (last 30 years) is +8.6%. China's Real Equity returns CAGR over the same period? -3.0%. This disconnect is historically unprecedented, there are 5 countries in modern history that went through something similar: China, Philippines, Hong Kong, Malaysia, and Korea. China sticks out like a sore thumb here - There are 2 historical parallels that I like to compare modern China to. The US in the 1960s when it was THE global leader in manufacturing and South Korea from 1977 up to the Asian Financial Crisis 1) US in the 1960s Pick any 5~10 year holding period in $SPX during the 1960s and you'll get subpar returns. A 10-year total return of ~45% (~3.8% CAGR) to negative in some cases if you panic sold during some of the dips. Imagine reading about how the US is the dominant manufacturer, is leading in innovation, and the equity markets being this soft all through the 60s. Then you get slammed with Stagflation in the 70s, and the US equity markets finally wakes up and blasts off in 1982. That's a long time waiting. The reason why I think China is like the US in the 1960s apart from both being the global leader in manufacturing is that in the 1960s in the US, the winners in the economy were Labor. Put simply, most of the excess value created by the economy accrued to Labor over Capital (stark difference vs. today as any excess value creation by the US economy primarily accrues to Capital now). You had 1 man working at the factory and it was enough to support a whole family, buy a house, go on vacation, everything. In China today.. this is somewhat true as 70%+ of Chinese Millennials own their homes, there are viral stories of food delivery drivers capable of supporting a family.. and while their life is tough, the important takeaway is that these things are possible and indicative to me that Labor in China are the primary beneficiaries of its economic expansion over Capital (side note: in general, I think how Economists calculate Labor share of economic output is wildly inaccurate). When does this unravel? Does it unravel? That's the multi million dollar question isn't it. My optimistic view is "tide that lifts all boats". One parallel is 1930s Germany is representative of both Labor and Capital winning during a period of capturing global manufacturing share. Germany's stock market did quite well (+23% in 1933, and in the following 7 years, 6 were positive all by double digits and the 1 negative year in 1938 was -2.5%) and at the same time, the German worker took vacations (KdF), owned their homes, etc. (modern Economists will show you these roundabout calculations of how Labor share of economic output decreased during this time but again, this is why I don't trust these calculations as being reflective of economic reality. It is undeniable that Labor in 1930s Germany had it extraordinarily good) My other view is that in a Capitalist system (which despite what people tell you, China is arguably more capitalist than America now), the Capital holders eventually win. It probably takes a crisis to trigger it though which brings me onto.. 2) South Korea and the Asian Financial Crisis From 1977 to 1996, South Korea's economy grew at a CAGR of ~9%, while real equity returns were ~4%. Then comes the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis that forced a bunch of corporate and financial restructuring (what essentially took place was a transfer of power so Capital can capture more of the economy's output going forward) then after 1998, KOSPI goes up 8x. 20 years later in 2017 looking back, real equity returns finally outpace GDP growth (~5.7% vs. ~4.1%). It took a crisis for Capital to take over.. is something similar going to happen with China? TL;DR I'm still bullish China long-term. Anyone who has taken the time to visit China like I have multiple times knows that they have arguably surpassed America already and we're basically going through a process of unwinding years of propaganda. Am I going to be a bagholder or a genius? Time will tell, but reality can only be ignored for so long It's undeniable that the Chinese decade or century is here. The question is still not an "IF", but a "When", despite how dog Chinese equities have been.

📊 SPX | Flujos 0DTE Aparece un put spread 0DTE de aproximadamente 6.000 contratos en los strikes 7.645/7.640, que aporta una ligera gamma positiva intradía. 📍 Esta zona podría actuar como soporte temporal si continúan las caídas, ayudando a amortiguar la presión vendedora. ⚠️ Recordemos que esta gamma desaparece con el vencimiento de hoy.
Por debajo de niveles clave las caídas se aceleran en SOX y NDX.

La clave es que la crisis de deuda francesa está dejando de ser un problema exclusivamente político para convertirse en un riesgo financiero para toda Europa. La rentabilidad a 10 años ha alcanzado el 5%, máximos desde 2002, mientras que el diferencial frente a Alemania se aproxima a los 160 puntos básicos, máximos de 15 años. Cerca de 100 gestores y operadores de deuda europea habrían salido de sus puestos tras el desplome de operaciones apalancadas con bonos franceses. Las ventas forzosas están agravando la caída. Muchos fondos mantenían posiciones similares en deuda italiana. Si necesitan reducir más riesgo, las ventas podrían contagiarse a los bonos italianos. El catalizador inmediato será la revisión de la calificación crediticia de Francia por Moody's, prevista para el viernes 23 de octubre.
